evidence: Words judged: 'Who has to step aside because they’re too close to it?' It is one question inserted second in the paragraph's list of process questions under 'When Somebody Has to Go'; SOURCE says nothing else in the paragraph is replaced, and CONTEXT shows it once, with the article's curly apostrophe. Against his line ('...who preserves evidence, who is recused, who decides temporary restrictions...') it is a plain-words form of 'who is recused'. The clause 'because they’re too close to it' only spells out what recusal is (stepping out of a decision over closeness or a conflict), so I do not count it as a new claim or fact. It sits right before 'Who decides to put temporary restrictions on someone?', which keeps his adjacency (recused, then who decides temporary restrictions). Reading the paragraph with it in: same register, length and 'Who ...?' shape as its neighbours, no seam, no hedge, no tidy summary, nothing that sounds like another writer. The 'it' has a referent: the paragraph already uses 'it' for the matter at hand ('before it’s about anyone in particular'), and 'too close to it' is an ordinary idiom (C02 fine). Tell rows T01 to T29 and C01 to C04 all checked on the draft in its paragraph. One row has something in it: T02. The paragraph is a run of one-line questions (eight with this one), which a skeptical editor will notice, and the writer's ledger calls it 'not part of a run', which I do not accept as stated. I count T02 PRESENT at paragraph level but justified: that run is how the paragraph is already built and is not new with this change, its items are his own list (SOURCE is the same list, with three 'who' clauses in a row too, so the 'Who' repeats in T26 are his), the draft adds his point and no new teaching beat, and folding recusal into a neighbouring question instead would make a packed T21 sentence. T09 and T13: the clause gives this question a reason its neighbours lack, so it is not equal-weight filler. Every other row is ABSENT (no first person, abstraction, bridge, closer, tic word, distinctive repeated word, invented fact or named-entity claim). Linter: CLEAR with no findings, so there is no label to resolve. Small nit, not a failure: 'recused' is his own word and would also fit; the plain phrasing matches the neighbouring questions.
